nodes.description: Without RIPK4, keratinocytes do not complete their differentiation program. Ripk4-null mice die perinatally with abnormal epidermal differentiation, the defect is cell autonomous to the keratinocyte lineage, and Ripk4-null skin grafted onto a normal host develops abnormal hair follicles and epidermal dysplasia. In the human disease this is the cellular basis for dysplasia of the ectodermal appendages (hair and nails) and for failed separation of epithelial surfaces.

nodes.description: Defective keratinocyte differentiation disturbs the ectodermal appendages built from keratinocytes. Ripk4-null skin grafted onto a normal host forms abnormal hair follicles, which underlies the sparse, curly, light-coloured scalp hair of CHAND syndrome. The nail dysplasia is attributed to the same keratinocyte differentiation defect in the nail unit by analogy; no study has examined the nail apparatus in RIPK4 deficiency.

nodes.description: RIPK4 sits in a transcriptional and signaling axis of surface ectoderm. p63, the master regulator of stratified epithelia mutated in AEC syndrome, directly activates RIPK4 transcription. RIPK4 in turn phosphorylates IRF6, the transcription factor mutated in Van der Woude and popliteal pterygium syndromes, at Ser413 and Ser424, activating it and moving it into the nucleus, where it induces the differentiation regulators GRHL3 and OVOL1. Loss of RIPK4 therefore weakens the IRF6-dependent differentiation program. This shared axis is why CHAND syndrome overlaps clinically with AEC syndrome (ankyloblepharon, ectodermal dysplasia) and why the RIPK4 and IRF6 pterygium syndromes resemble each other.

nodes.description: The periderm is a transient superficial epithelial layer that keeps apposed embryonic epithelia, including the eyelid margins, from adhering. In Ripk4-deficient mice periderm development is abnormal and E-cadherin is mislocalized to the apical membrane of the outer peridermal cells, so epithelial surfaces fuse; all external orifices are fused in the knockout, and the fusions depend on E-cadherin. Ankyloblepharon in CHAND syndrome is the human manifestation of this defect at the eyelid margins; in the severe, kinase-domain RIPK4 disease the same failure also produces oral synechiae and pterygia.

nodes.description: RIPK4 is an ankyrin-repeat serine/threonine kinase expressed in keratinocytes and required for their differentiation. In CHAND syndrome both alleles carry p.Glu284Lys, just outside the kinase domain. The kinase-domain variants that cause Bartsocas-Papas syndrome abolish catalytic activity in reporter assays; the CHAND variant has not been tested, and the proposal that it is a partial loss of function explaining the milder phenotype is an inference from its position.

evidence.snippet: Alternatively, CHAND and Bartsocas-Papas syndrome might be allelic disorders or RIPK4 mutations could confer varying degrees of phenotypic severity, depending on their localization within or outside functionally important domains.

nodes.description: Constitutive Ripk4 knockout. The mice die perinatally with abnormal epidermal differentiation and fusion of external orifices. As a null, it models the severe end of the RIPK4 allelic series (Bartsocas-Papas syndrome) more closely than the hypomorphic CHAND genotype.
Scalp hair is sparse as well as curly in the RIPK4-confirmed patients.

nodes.description: Homozygous missense variant found in the three affected children of the Kuwaiti kindred and in the independent CHAND patient reported by Busa and colleagues. It lies just C-terminal to the serine/threonine kinase domain, whereas the Bartsocas-Papas syndrome missense variants cluster inside that domain; the original authors proposed this location as the reason for the milder phenotype. No functional assay of p.Glu284Lys has been reported.
